sixteen down the river

By: Tarryn Crossman | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Summary:
It’s one of the toughest endurance canoeing races in the world, 3 days of gruelling paddling, carrying, and focusing. Andy Birkett is the only human to have ever won the race 16 times. “Nothing is given in the Dusi; you have to earn your way down the river every day”
This is the story beyond the river. It has taken the boy who first paddled the Dusi solo at 13, to become the man who finished first 16 times.
If you ask anyone to describe Andy, the first word is always humble. But humility doesn’t make you a world champion athlete, or does it?
In 2022, he thought his career was over. Asthma, poor performance results and younger guns taking more titles. But then he pushed harder, and with every burst of doubt, he pushed harder and took the world games championships
He is an elite athlete, father and husband, which comes first? How do they come together, and can the river teach us all something about life?

Script:


(Archive Dusi Canoe Marathon) A glorious morning in Pietermaritzburg for the 75th Dusi.



(Govan) The Dusi Canoe Marathon is one of the toughest river races there is. For over 75 years, thousands of paddlers from around the world travel to the Valley of a Thousand Hills in KwaZulu‑Natal to paddle a 120 kilometres from Pietermaritzburg to Durban. It’s a three-day race of relentless paddling and gruelling portages over rugged terrain.



(Archive Dusi Canoe Marathon) Birkett and Fenn looking strong through the rapids and with a real chance to repeat their win of 2024.



(Andy Birkett) As a schoolboy, you see everyone racing past and I probably, at the age of ten when I was at Merchiston, said to a mate, “We're going to win this race one day.” The cocky little youngster.



(Govan) Andy Birkett first competed in the Dusi as a tiny 13-year-old. He was barely strong enough to carry his paddle ski.



(Andy Birkett) We had no idea where we're busy going. You get a sticker on your boat if you've done ten, 20 or 30 Dusis.



(Govan) Ja.



(Andy Birkett) And we learned that was the best navigating advice is if you saw an old guy with a 30-sticker on his boat, you follow him no matter what.



(Govan) This was the beginning of Andy’s lifelong love affair with the Dusi Marathon. He would go on to win the race multiple times, which is no small task. The Dusi takes no prisoners. It's the ultimate equaliser.



(Andy Birkett) It doesn't matter…



(Govan) It's not an easy river.



(Andy Birkett) …where are you from or what you've done. When you in the race in the valley, it's a serious challenge and you have to go through that and work out how to get yourself down the river.



(Archive Dusi Canoe Marathon) Then signalled a 14th Dusi Canoe Marathon title for a legend of the race, Andy Burkitt. He partnered this year with Matt Fenn as the pair, based in East London, powered their way to the finish at Blue Lagoon on day three.



(Govan) How does doing that sport affect your mindset?



(Andy Birkett) I like to think I don't panic when I'm busy racing. But I think that we all have triggers in life. I was joking with Matt Fenn, we've raced the last two Dusis together. And on our way to winning, we took a compulsory portage. We tried to find a path back to the river and I couldn't find the river.



(Govan) You couldn't find the Dusi.



(Andy Birkett) It was just thick bushes and I couldn't get back to the river. And I was absolute panic mode, I wasn't calm at all. Matt just said to me, “If we can see the river through the bushes, we can get there.” So, we just crawled for about 50 metres through this dense bush to get back to the river.



(Govan) And did you win?



(Andy Birkett) Ja, we won.



(Govan) Was that your first win?



(Andy Birkett) No, no. That was two years ago, that was after about 13.



(Govan) Thirteen years, stuff like that still happens when you can't find the river.



(Andy Birkett) Ja, ja, ja.



(Govan) Bro. It's the same river, though, ja.



(Andy Birkett) Ja, I'm a slow learner. A slow learner.



(Govan) This year, Andy Birkett came to the Valley with one goal: he didn’t just want to win, he wanted to become the only human to ever win the Dusi 16 times.



(Archive Dusi Canoe Marathon) No one has ever done what Andy Birkett is going to do today. Andy Birkett has done it, his 16th Dusi win.



(Govan) And just like that, Andy Birkett becomes an elite athlete for the history books. Sixteen Dusi Marathon wins at the age of 35.



(Govan) Andy, how did you end up winning 16 times?



(Andy Birkett) I don’t know. I just enjoy it and I feel like it's almost a problem‑solving scenario. Each year, you're faced with different variables in your life. And I love training, I love racing the Dusi and fit that into the summer. It's a lovely thing to do.



(Govan) Today I’m going paddling with a Dusi legend. No pressure.



(Govan) Is this the equipment you use to compete?



(Andy Birkett) It is my Dusi paddle.



(Govan) Oh, this is the Dusi paddle?



(Andy Birkett) Ja, ja, nice thick edges for the rocks. And then my flat water paddle. So, you will use my Dusi paddle. Ja, that's what we're going to use today.



(Govan) It is a good thing you already won it. I don't want to put any bad luck on you.



(Govan) Why do you paddle?



(Andy Birket) I think I enjoy the challenge. When I set myself a goal, say I want to win World Marathon Champs, or I want to win the Dusi. It's not just about the race, it's about the journey. And it's also nice to walk that journey with someone else.



(Govan) Nine of Andy’s Dusi Canoe Marathon wins have been in a double ski. To get there took more than just training. It took months of living together, studying each other, until they moved as one.



(Andy Birkett) If you don't understand the other person, you can't work as a team effectively. When you're actually busy racing and you're busy training as well, that positive energy in the boat is so important, because I normally say, you can get two people in a boat, and it's one plus one equals two. Or if you combine well, you can actually almost make it exponential and one plus one equals three. And it can also go the other way, that one plus one equals one and a half. And it's like it doesn't work, it humbles you.



(Govan) What makes a good second?



(Andy Birkett) A selfless person. Someone whose only goal is to make sure that boat goes as fast as it can. Not, "I want to try and be the best or it's all about me."



(Govan) And does your wife paddle with you?



(Andy Birkett) Yes, yes, yes.



(Govan) Is she your favourite person to paddle with?



(Andy Birkett) Are the mics on? No, Nix is definitely my favourite person to paddle with.



(Andy Birkett) You want some coffee?



(Nicky Birkett) I’d love some coffee, thank you. What's the plan for the day, Andrew James?



(Andy Birkett) What have the boys got today?



(Nicky Birkett) Dave's got a playdate after school and then Danny, he finishes at one.



(Andy Birkett) Does he finish at one?



(Nicky Birkett) Ja.



(Andy Birkett) You got some milk?



(Nicky Birkett) Ja, thank you. Is this mine?



(Andy Birkett) Yes.



(Nicky Birkett) This is a strong coffee, Andrew James.



(Andy Birkett) Is it?



(Nicky Birkett) Ja.



(Govan) When they met, Andy's wife Nicky was mainly a sea paddler, while Andy focused on rivers. But over the years, they’ve raced together in flat waters and rough seas, becoming a solid team in paddling and life.



(Govan) What role do you think paddling plays in your relationship?



(Nicky Birkett) I think it's a massive part of our relationship because to compete at Andy's level and to perform consistently…



(Govan) Ja?



(Nicky Birkett) It takes a lot of discipline and he's an incredibly competitive, driven, focused human. I mean, he doesn't miss a beat.



(Govan) It must take a lot of sacrifice from you guys?



(Nicky Birkett) It does take a lot of sacrifice, but Andy is incredible with time management. So, when he's with the family, it's like his focus is on the family. And when he's paddling, it's paddling. And everything's done in the early mornings, you know, before anyone is up.



(Govan) Listening to Nix talk about Andy's dedication to the sport, it's hard to believe that, at some point, he wanted to pack it all in.



(Nicky Birkett) He drove us all insane. He's got to keep training, like we are so happy with Andy training.



(Govan) How was it when he wasn't paddling?



(Nicky Birkett) He started monitoring everything we did, you know, everything. You know, the flour has gone down this much and that's like…



(Andy Birkett) I remember Nix pulled me aside and said, “You need to find another goal, you need to find something to work towards.” I regrouped and trained really hard, went to World Games, won the gold medal at World Games and the World Marathon Champs that following year.



(Govan) He may be a perfectionist paddler, but when you see Andy, the dad, out in the waves with his boys, David and Daniel, he’s a big kid.
(Andy Birkett) Danny, are you catching bombers? You ready? Are you? Are you sure?
(Andy Birkett) I hope to race one day with my boys – it would be so nice to take them down there.
(Govan) You think you'll ever stop racing the Dusi?
(Andy Birkett) I think if I'm doing it, I'm racing it. I can't not race.



(Govan) You're going to be those ballies with the 30 stickers on the boat and the laaities are going to be following you.
